Imputing a dataset's gaps

Source: vignettes/articles/gap-fitting.Rmd
gap-fitting.Rmd

A dataset rarely lacks a variable on every plot. Most plots carry a survey year, coordinates or an elevation, and some do not. The plots that carry it are labelled examples from the same surveys, recorded by the same people, as the plots that lack it. Gap fitting reads them: on the plots where the value is recorded (the complete plots) it chooses how to combine the model’s imputed value with the dataset’s own neighbours, and applies that choice to the plots where it is missing (the gaps). The model’s imputed value is never replaced; the fitted value comes back beside it, with a report of what was chosen and why.

This article covers the candidates gap fitting chooses among, how the choice is tested at the distance the gaps actually are, fitting a single model’s imputed values, reading the report, model suites and the command line, the settings, and the gaps the dataset cannot inform.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/resolve/r")

# The RESOLVE engine library, downloaded once
library(resolveR)
resolve.install_backend()
pip install resolve-core

What gap fitting chooses among

Seven candidates impute a gap, from the dataset alone, from the model alone, or from both:

  • local_constant: the complete plots’ mean (their median on a log scale, their mean direction for a bearing, their geographic median for a location);
  • resolve: the model’s imputed value as it stands;
  • offset_slope: the model’s imputed value calibrated on the complete plots, y = mean(y) + b (raw - mean(raw)), with b fitted by least squares; b = 1 shifts the imputed value by its mean error there, b = 0 is the local constant;
  • knn_species: the median recorded value of the k complete plots most similar in species composition (the Ochiai similarity of their species lists);
  • knn_spatial: the median recorded value of the k nearest complete plots by great-circle distance;
  • stack_species and stack_species_spatial: the model’s imputed value and those neighbour medians combined by least squares on the complete plots.

k is chosen from 1, 3, 5, 10, 20 and 50 by how well the neighbours impute the complete plots.

Testing the choice at the gaps’ distance

A complete plot’s nearest other complete plots are as near as complete plots are to one another. A gap can be much farther from them: a region nobody georeferenced, or the oldest surveys. Judging the neighbours by how well they impute a complete plot from its own nearest plots would trust them more than they deserve at the gaps.

Gap fitting therefore judges the candidates by cross-validation over the complete plots, with folds laid out so that a held-out plot lies as far from the plots it may read as a gap lies from the complete plots (k-fold nearest-neighbour distance matching, Linnenbrink et al. 2024). Each gap’s distance to its nearest complete plot is measured on every axis it can be measured on: species similarity, km where the gaps carry coordinates, and survey years where they carry a year. The complete plots are grouped into squares of an equal-area map, into survey-year periods, into both, or one by one, at a range of sizes, and the groups are dealt out to ten folds. Where the gaps lie farther away than any fold can, a held-out plot also loses every plot within a buffer, and each plot’s buffer is the distances of one gap drawn at random. The layout whose held-out plots match the gaps’ distances most closely is the one used.

Every fitted part is fitted on the other folds: a held-out plot’s neighbours, the least-squares coefficients and k. A complete plot left with no neighbour counts as imputed by the local constant, which is all the dataset says about it there. Each candidate is scored on the out-of-fold values by the target’s own error: the mean absolute error, on a log scale that of log1p, the circular error of a bearing, the median distance in km for a location. The candidate with the lowest error is fitted again on every complete plot and imputes the gaps.

The lowest of seven errors reads lower than the error the chosen method then makes. The report therefore estimates the error of the whole choice by repeating it with each fold held out and scoring it on that fold (nested cross-validation).

Gaps with coordinates and gaps without them choose apart: the second group only among the candidates that read no position.

The survey and its gaps

The examples use the survey of 150 plots in the Alps that ships with the R package. A model trained on another survey imputes plots it never saw, so the first 75 plots train it and the other 75 are the dataset whose elevation has gaps: every fifth of them lacks its recorded elevation.

plots <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "plots.csv", package = "resolveR"))
species <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "species.csv", package = "resolveR"))

is_training <- seq_len(nrow(plots)) <= 75
train_plots <- plots[is_training, ]
train_species <- species[species$plot_id %in% train_plots$plot_id, ]
my_plots <- plots[!is_training, ]
my_species <- species[species$plot_id %in% my_plots$plot_id, ]

is_gap <- seq_len(nrow(my_plots)) %% 5 == 0
my_plots$elevation_recorded <- ifelse(is_gap, NA, my_plots$elevation)
c(complete = sum(!is_gap), gaps = sum(is_gap))
#> complete     gaps 
#>       60       15
import os
import tempfile

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import resolve_core as rc

data = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gcol33/resolve/master/r/inst/extdata/"
plots = pd.read_csv(data + "plots.csv")
species = pd.read_csv(data + "species.csv")

is_training = plots.index < 75
train_plots = plots[is_training]
train_species = species[species.plot_id.isin(train_plots.plot_id)]
my_plots = plots[~is_training].reset_index(drop=True)
my_species = species[species.plot_id.isin(my_plots.plot_id)]

is_gap = (my_plots.index + 1) % 5 == 0
my_plots["elevation_recorded"] = my_plots.elevation.where(~is_gap)
{"complete": int((~is_gap).sum()), "gaps": int(is_gap.sum())}
#> {'complete': 60, 'gaps': 15}

The model imputes elevation from the species alone and is saved to a checkpoint.

roles <- list(plot_id = "plot_id", species_id = "species",
              abundance = "cover", genus = "genus", family = "family")
targets <- list(elevation = list(column = "elevation", task = "regression"))
dataset <- resolve.dataset.frame(train_plots, train_species,
                                 roles = roles, targets = targets)
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "elevation.pt")
fit <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, maxEpochs = 100L,
                             savePath = path, verbose = FALSE)
roles = rc.RoleMapping()
roles.plot_id = "plot_id"
roles.species_id = "species"
roles.abundance = "cover"
roles.genus = "genus"
roles.family = "family"
dataset = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(train_plots, train_species, roles,
                                        [rc.TargetSpec.regression("elevation")])

model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
train_config = rc.TrainConfig()
train_config.max_epochs = 100
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, train_config)
trainer.prepare_data(dataset)
result = trainer.fit()
path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "elevation.pt")
trainer.save(path, trainer.run_metadata)

The dataset’s plots are encoded with the model’s vocabularies and imputed, all of them: the complete plots are what the choice is tested on.

predictor <- resolve.load(path)
my_data <- resolve.dataset.frame(my_plots[c("plot_id", "lat", "lon")], my_species,
                                 roles = roles, vocabs = predictor$vocabs(),
                                 config = predictor$dataset_config())
preds <- resolve.predict.dataset(predictor, my_data)
predictor = rc.Predictor.load(path)
header_csv = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "my_plots.csv")
species_csv = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "my_species.csv")
my_plots[["plot_id", "lat", "lon"]].to_csv(header_csv, index=False)
my_species.to_csv(species_csv, index=False)
my_data = rc.ResolveDataset.from_csv_with_vocabs(
    header_csv, species_csv, roles, [],
    predictor.external_vocabs, predictor.dataset_config)
preds = predictor.predict_dataset(my_data)

Gap fitting with a single model

Gap fitting reads the dataset’s own tables: the species records, for composition over every species they name, whatever the model’s vocabulary holds; the coordinates, for the spatial neighbours; and the column holding the recorded value, empty on the gaps. targets names each target to fit and how its values lie, here elevation on its own scale.

columns <- list(plot_id = "plot_id", species_id = "species",
                latitude = "lat", longitude = "lon",
                recorded = list(elevation = "elevation_recorded"))
fits <- resolve.fit_prediction_gaps(preds, my_species, my_plots, columns = columns,
                                    targets = list(elevation = list(scale = "linear")))
elevation <- fits$elevation
table(elevation$method)
#> 
#>              recorded stack_species_spatial 
#>                    60                    15
columns = {"plot_id": "plot_id", "species_id": "species",
           "latitude": "lat", "longitude": "lon",
           "recorded": {"elevation": "elevation_recorded"}}
fits = rc.fit_prediction_gaps(preds, my_species, my_plots, columns=columns,
                              targets={"elevation": {"scale": "linear"}})
elevation = fits["elevation"]
pd.Series(elevation.method).value_counts()
#> recorded         60
#> stack_species    15
#> Name: count, dtype: int64

A complete plot keeps its recorded value (recorded); every gap carries the method that imputed it. The gaps’ recorded elevation is known here, so the fitted values can be checked against it beside the model’s own imputed value.

order <- match(preds$plot_ids, my_plots$plot_id)
truth <- my_plots$elevation[order]
gaps <- is.na(my_plots$elevation_recorded[order])
c(model = mean(abs(preds$predictions$elevation[gaps] - truth[gaps])),
  fitted = mean(abs(elevation$fitted[gaps] - truth[gaps])))
#>    model   fitted 
#> 274.8799 154.4564
order = pd.Index(my_plots.plot_id.astype(str)).get_indexer(list(preds.plot_ids))
truth = my_plots.elevation.to_numpy()[order]
gaps = my_plots.elevation_recorded.isna().to_numpy()[order]
raw = preds.predictions["elevation"].numpy()
fitted = elevation.fitted.numpy()
{"model": float(np.abs(raw[gaps] - truth[gaps]).mean()),
 "fitted": float(np.abs(fitted[gaps] - truth[gaps]).mean())}
#> {'model': 252.3594970703125, 'fitted': 150.94150117990975}

Reading the report

The report says what was chosen and why: the number of complete plots and gaps, the gaps’ distance to their nearest complete plot on each axis, the fold layout, the k each kind of neighbour chose, and per group of gaps every candidate’s cross-validated error (cv_error), the error estimated for the whole choice (estimated_error), the method chosen and what it fitted.

located <- elevation$report$groups$located
located$method
#> [1] "stack_species_spatial"
round(unlist(located$cv_error), 1)
#>        local_constant               resolve          offset_slope 
#>                 576.0                 158.6                 160.4 
#>           knn_species         stack_species           knn_spatial 
#>                 121.5                 109.5                 580.8 
#> stack_species_spatial 
#>                 108.4
round(located$estimated_error, 1)
#> [1] 111.2
elevation$report$axes$km$gap_distance$median
#> [1] 7.379892
located = elevation.report["groups"]["located"]
located["method"]
#> stack_species
{m: round(e, 1) for m, e in located["cv_error"].items()}
#> {'local_constant': 576.0, 'resolve': 167.7, 'offset_slope': 171.9, 'knn_species': 121.5, 'stack_species': 114.4, 'knn_spatial': 580.8, 'stack_species_spatial': 115.6}
round(located["estimated_error"], 1)
#> 119.3
elevation.report["axes"]["km"]["gap_distance"]["median"]
#> 7.379891561267665

folds gives the layout the choice was judged on: the number of folds, the side of the squares (block_km) and the length of the survey-year periods (block_years), the median buffer in km and in years, and how far the held-out plots’ distances still lie from the gaps’ on each axis (mismatch: the Wasserstein distance between the two distributions on the rank scale of both together, from 0 where they match to 1 where they do not overlap).

A chosen least-squares method also reports its coefficients (coefficients, one per term: resolve, species, spatial), the complete plots it was fitted on (n_fitted) and the k of each neighbour term. For a bearing a coefficient is a complex number, reported as its modulus (how much it shrinks the term) and its angle_deg (how far it turns it).

Model suites and the command line

A suite fits its targets after combining its members. columns names the recorded column of each target to fit (two, latitude and longitude, for a location) and optionally the survey-year column; the imputation table then carries <target>_fitted and <target>_fit_method beside <target>, and each fitted target a gap_fit with its report. The scale follows the target: a bearing is fitted as a direction, a location in a plane, a target the members learned on log1p on that scale.

suite <- resolve.load_suite("resolve-suite")
preds <- resolve.predict.suite(
  suite, species = my_species, header = my_plots,
  columns = list(recorded = list(year = "Year", location = c("Latitude", "Longitude")),
                 survey_year = "Year"),
  gapFitting = TRUE)
head(as.data.frame(preds)[c("plot_id", "year", "year_fitted", "year_fit_method")])
preds$targets$year$gap_fit$report$groups
suite = rc.SuitePredictor.load("resolve-suite")
preds = suite.predict(
    my_species, my_plots,
    columns={"recorded": {"year": "Year", "location": ["Latitude", "Longitude"]},
             "survey_year": "Year"},
    gap_fitting=True)
preds.to_pandas()[["plot_id", "year", "year_fitted", "year_fit_method"]].head()
preds.target("year").gap_fit.report["groups"]

These lines are shown and not run here. On the command line, --fit-gaps with one --recorded per target does the same for --suite and for --model, and writes the report beside the imputed values:

resolve predict --suite resolve-suite --header plots.csv --species species.csv \
  --fit-gaps --recorded year=Year --recorded location=Latitude,Longitude \
  --survey-year Year --output predictions.csv
# predictions.csv: <target>_fitted and <target>_fit_method beside each target
# predictions.csv.gap_fitting.json: the report (--gap-report names another path)

With --model, a target is the prediction head of its name, on a log scale when the model learned it on log1p; --gap-target aspect=circular:360:asp_sin,asp_cos or --gap-target location=geographic:lat,lon names the scale and the heads otherwise.

<target>_fit_method reads recorded on the plots that record the target, so it also tells which values were imputed. Without gap fitting, the recorded columns alone (columns$recorded in R, columns["recorded"] in Python, --recorded without --fit-gaps) add <target>_recorded instead: TRUE where the plot records the target, FALSE where <target> is imputed.

Settings

Seven settings change the choice (gapFitting in R, gap_fitting in Python, the --gap-* flags on the command line):

  • candidates: the methods to choose among, by name; the gaps without coordinates need at least one that reads no position;
  • k_grid: the neighbour counts k is chosen from;
  • spatial = FALSE (--no-spatial): composition only, no spatial neighbours;
  • n_folds: the number of folds, 10 by default; the estimated error needs at least 3;
  • max_fold_share: the largest share of the complete plots one fold may hold, 0.5 by default;
  • matching_sample: the number of complete plots the layouts are compared on, 1000 by default;
  • matching_seed: the seed of the order the groups are dealt out in, the buffers drawn and the complete plots compared.
composition_only <- resolve.fit_prediction_gaps(
  preds, my_species, my_plots, columns = columns,
  targets = list(elevation = list(scale = "linear")),
  gapFitting = list(spatial = FALSE, k_grid = c(1, 3, 5, 10)))
composition_only$elevation$report$groups$unlocated$method
#> [1] "stack_species"
config = rc.GapFittingConfig()
config.spatial = False
config.k_grid = [1, 3, 5, 10]
composition_only = rc.fit_prediction_gaps(preds, my_species, my_plots, columns=columns,
                                          targets={"elevation": {"scale": "linear"}},
                                          gap_fitting=config)
composition_only["elevation"].report["groups"]["unlocated"]["method"]
#> stack_species

resolve.fit_gaps() (R) and rc.fit_gaps() (Python) take the same choice on vectors: the raw imputed value, the recorded values, a matrix of species and optionally the coordinates and survey years, for a value imputed anywhere.

Gaps the dataset cannot inform

The complete plots show how far off a gap’s candidates are only where the gaps resemble them. Two kinds of gap do not:

  • Undated plots that are probably older than the dated ones. When the undated plots are the oldest surveys, nothing on the dated plots shows how far off they are, and the model’s own imputed value is the better estimate: keep <target> rather than <target>_fitted for them. For other targets an old survey is visible through the survey-year axis, and gap fitting allows for it.
  • Plots without coordinates that probably come from an area with no georeferenced plots. A location’s gaps have no position, so the folds are matched in species similarity and survey year only, and a missing region still looks near in species terms. Such plots are better served by the model’s imputed value, or by the species stack alone.
